parts:
Hello,

I have a (maybe naive) question.

Starting from the subsection "11.1. Bayesian Measurement Error Model" of the Stan manual

I would like to know if it's possible in principle to apply the following model

model {
x ~ normal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior
y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);
...
}

with alpha and beta as data vectors and x as real parameter

Thanks.
Stefano

Hello Andrew,
yes it works in the NON vectorized version

=======================================
data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
real alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real alpha_2[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real alpha_3[N]; // predictor (covariate)

real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma; // outcome noise

real<lower=0> x[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x; // prior scale

real<lower=0> x_2[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x_2; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x_2; // prior scale

real<lower=0> x_3[N]; // unknown true value
real<lower=0> mu_x_3; // prior location
real<lower=0> sigma_x_3; // prior scale

}
model {
x ~ normal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior

x_2 ~ normal(mu_x_2, sigma_x_2); // prior
x_3 ~ normal(mu_x_3, sigma_x_3); // prior

for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal( (alpha[n] * x[n]) + (alpha_2[n] * x_2[n]) + (alpha_3[n] * x_3[n]), sigma);
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}
=======================================



But it does not work in the vectorized form (it's obviously possible I'm missing something..)

=======================================
data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
    int<lower=0> K; // number of cases
    vector[K] alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
    real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma; // outcome noise

    vector<lower=0>[K] x[N]; // unknown true value
    vector<lower=0>[K] mu_x; // prior location
    vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_x; // prior scale

}
model {
    vector[K] temp;
    for(k in 1:K) x[k] ~ normal(mu_x[k], sigma_x[k]); // prior
   
    for(n in 1:N) {
        for(k in 1:K)  temp[k] = alpha[n,k] * x[n,k];
        y[n] ~ normal( sum(temp), sigma);

    }
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}
=======================================



Thanks!

messages.author: fa6f5d4c13c0cca5
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 11.1. Bayesian Measurement Error Model - variation on this example
parts: This line:
for(k in 1:K) x[k] ~ normal(mu_x[k], sigma_x[k])

Isn't looping like you want it to. Instead of putting a prior on x[k][1:N], you're putting it on x[1:K][k]. You need to redefine x as either a matrix or a K-length array of N-length vectors to get the expected result.

parts:
After I verified it worked for a linear combination of normally distributed variables

e.g., y = normal(..,..) * 0.5 + normal(..,..) * 0.1 + normal(..,..) * 0.4




I tried to solve the same problem for LOGnormally distributed variables

e.g., y = LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.5 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.1 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.4

Code, below. However the inference does not have the same performances. Why(?):

1) The problem might itself be harder
2) I have a bug in the code

==================================================
library(MCMCpack)
alpha = rdirichlet(100, c(10,4,1))


x = exp(rnorm(100, 5,0.5))
x_2 = exp(rnorm(100, 2,0.5))
x_3 = exp(rnorm(100, 8,1))

y = (alpha[,1] * x) + (alpha[,2] * x_2) + (alpha[,3] * x_3)

m = "

data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
int<lower=0> K; // number of cases
vector[K] alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
}
parameters {

real<lower=0.00001> sigma; // outcome noise
vector<lower=0.00001>[K] sigma_x; // prior scale

vector<lower=0>[K] x[N]; // unknown true value
vector<lower=0>[K] mu_x; // prior location

}

model {
vector[K] temp;
for(n in 1:N) x[n] ~ lognormal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior

for(n in 1:N) {
for(k in 1:K)  temp[k] = log(alpha[n,k]) + log(x[n,k]);
y[n] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(temp), sigma);
}
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2);
sigma_x ~ normal(0.75, 0.3);  //test values
mu_x ~ normal(5,2);  //test values
}
"

fit <- rstan:::stan(
    model_code =m,
    data=list(y=y, alpha = alpha, K = 3, N=100),
    control=list(adapt_delta=0.999, stepsize = 0.01, max_treedepth =15)
)

==================================================



Thanks!

Stefano Mangiola

Data analyst (MSc, MPhil, PhD candidate)
@ Melbourne University
Hovens lab - Papenfuss lab
Royal Melbourne Hospital - WEHI

>

> I tried to solve the same problem for LOGnormally distributed variables
>
> e.g., y = LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.5 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.1 + LOGnormal(..,..) * 0.4
>
> Code, below. However the inference does not have the same performances. Why(?):
>
> 1) The problem might itself be harder
> 2) I have a bug in the code
>
> ==================================================
> library(MCMCpack)
> alpha = rdirichlet(100, c(10,4,1))
>
>
> x = exp(rnorm(100, 5,0.5))
> x_2 = exp(rnorm(100, 2,0.5))
> x_3 = exp(rnorm(100, 8,1))
>
> y = (alpha[,1] * x) + (alpha[,2] * x_2) + (alpha[,3] * x_3)

This is very confusing for me. For one, this isn't simulating
from the model you're talking about because you add an extra
layer of uncertainty with that Dirichlet. Then do a ton of work
that's not necessary. Instead, you want a multinomial sample
with alpha = (0.5, 0.1, 0.4), then plug those indexes into
your mean and sd to generate without the extra work.

>
> m = "
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
> int<lower=0> K; // number of cases
> vector[K] alpha[N]; // predictor (covariate)
> real y[N]; // outcome (variate)
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0.00001> sigma; // outcome noise
> vector<lower=0.00001>[K] sigma_x; // prior scale
> vector<lower=0>[K] x[N]; // unknown true value
> vector<lower=0>[K] mu_x; // prior location
>
> }
> model {
> vector[K] temp;
> for(n in 1:N) x[n] ~ lognormal(mu_x, sigma_x); // prior
>
> for(n in 1:N) {
> for(k in 1:K) temp[k] = log(alpha[n,k]) + log(x[n,k]);
> y[n] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(temp), sigma);

The log_sum_exp should go on the outside! It's a mixture of
lognormals, not a lognormal with a mixed mean.

- Bob
